intro: Day-zero doubts, before you've written anything: whether this costs money, whether you need a card, which accounts to create, whether your computer is up to it, how much time a day it takes, who reads what you write, and what each part of this portal is.

preguntas.q: Is this going to cost me money?
preguntas.a: You can start today without paying anything. For the first few weeks the free version of ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini is enough, and the other accounts used here have free plans. As the course goes on, most people end up paying for a subscription to a single AI, which runs around €23 a month, and that's plenty. Prices change every few months, so check the official website of each service before deciding. The only thing that can give you a real scare is pay-per-use with an API key, and you won't even touch that in the first lessons.
preguntas.corta: You can start for free. Paying comes later, and it's optional.

preguntas.q: Do I have to enter my card to get started?
preguntas.a: No, and in fact you'd best not enter it yet. The accounts you need on day one are created with an email and a password, no card required. The card only shows up if you decide to pay for a subscription, and by then you'll already know why you're doing it. There's one situation where you should never enter it: if in the middle of a conversation the AI itself tells you to create an API key and paste in a card, stop and leave it for later. That's where people have gotten hit with scares of hundreds of euros, and the course calmly explains how to set a hard cap before you touch anything.
preguntas.corta: No. Day-one accounts don't ask for a card.

preguntas.q: How many accounts do I need to create? I hate having accounts everywhere.
preguntas.a: Three, and not all on the same day. An AI to talk to, which is ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini — one is enough. A GitHub account, where your project's files are stored along with their change history, and it doesn't ask for a card. And a Vercel account, the company that takes what's on GitHub and puts it online; its entry plan, Hobby, doesn't ask for a card either. You need the first one today; the other two when you get to the saving-and-publishing part. Use the same email for all three and write down where you signed up.
preguntas.corta: Three: an AI, GitHub, and Vercel. And not all today.

preguntas.q: Is the free version enough, or will I get stuck halfway?
preguntas.a: It's enough to get started. The free version lets you ask questions, paste in text, and see how it responds, which is exactly what you do at the beginning. What you'll notice is the cap: after a certain number of messages it tells you to wait a while, and in some cases it quietly switches you to a weaker model. That's when it makes sense to pay, not before. And one important thing: when you hit the limit of the free version or the subscription, you get throttled, not overcharged.
preguntas.corta: Yes, to get started. The cap is on messages, not on your bill.

preguntas.q: Do I have to pay for ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all at once?
preguntas.a: No, and paying for several on day one is one of the most expensive mistakes people make here. All three do almost the same thing for eighty percent of what you'll think to ask them, so pick one and stick with it for a few weeks. Switching from one to another costs nothing: there's no lock-in, nothing to move, and your old conversations stay right where they were. Once you've used it for a while, you'll be able to say in your own words what you ask each one for, and only then does it make sense to pay for a second one.
preguntas.corta: No. Just one, and a few weeks before you consider another.

preguntas.q: My computer is seven years old. Will it work?
preguntas.a: It'll work. Almost everything in the first few months happens inside the browser: the AI doesn't run on your computer, it runs on theirs, and you just type and read. What you do need is an up-to-date browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari) and a decent connection. It doesn't matter if it's an old or low-end laptop, and you don't need any special graphics card. Hardware only starts to matter if you later get into running models on your own machine, and that's neither on the main path nor something you need.
preguntas.corta: Yes. An up-to-date browser is enough for the first few months.

preguntas.q: Can I do all this from my phone or tablet?
preguntas.a: Some of it, yes; some, no. Reading the lessons, talking to the AI, and trying out prompts work perfectly well from your phone, and the apps handle that fine. What will trip you up is what comes after: organizing folders, looking at files, copying long texts from one place to another, and watching your project run on screen. That calls for a computer with a keyboard and a screen big enough for two windows. Rule of thumb: phone for reading and thinking in the checkout line, computer for actually doing.
preguntas.corta: For reading and asking, yes. For building the project, a computer.

preguntas.q: How much time a day do I need to put in? I have a job.
preguntas.a: Half an hour a day works well. Each lesson is designed to take twenty to thirty minutes, and it tells you at the top how long. What really makes the difference isn't a long Sunday session, it's consistency: four days of half an hour add up to far more than one four-hour afternoon, because you learn this by trying and getting it wrong, and that takes sleeping between one attempt and the next. If you only have ten minutes one day, read the lesson and leave the tasks for tomorrow. And don't do two lessons in a row on day one out of enthusiasm.
preguntas.corta: Half an hour a day. Four short days beats one long afternoon.

preguntas.q: Do I need to know how to code? Because I don't, and I'm not planning to learn.
preguntas.a: You don't need to, and you won't learn to code here. You don't write code: you hand the job to the AI and learn to check that what it gave you actually works. What you will practice is explaining yourself clearly, putting your data in front of it, and catching in time when something's wrong. It's more like directing a very fast, scatterbrained intern than studying computer science. You will see code on screen, and it's impressive at first; after two weeks you'll look at it the way you look at a car engine: you know what it does without knowing how to build one.
preguntas.corta: No. You commission and check; you don't write the code.

preguntas.q: What about English? Mine isn't great.
preguntas.a: You can do the whole course in your own language. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini understand and respond fine in any major language, and they reply in whatever language you write to them in. What you will run into in English are things that don't get translated: some tool buttons, folder names, and above all, error messages. There's a great workaround: copy the English text, paste it to the AI, and ask it to explain it to you in your own language. Nothing here depends on knowing English.
preguntas.corta: Not required. Whatever shows up in English, paste it to the AI.

preguntas.q: Does anyone read what I write in the chat?
preguntas.a: No person is sitting there reading it. But your conversations are stored on the company's servers, and on free and personal plans they can be used to train the models unless you turn that off in Settings. That's the first thing you should touch: go into your account settings, find the option about model improvement or training, and turn it off. It takes two minutes. On top of that, some services keep what you write for a while to review for abuse, so the sensible rule is simple: don't paste anything you'd mind seeing published.
preguntas.corta: It's stored, and can train the model. Turn it off in Settings.

preguntas.q: Can I paste my clients' data in so it can help me?
preguntas.a: Not as-is, no. A customer list, a payslip, an ID number, a medical report, or a contract with real names doesn't get pasted into a chat without first checking the training box and knowing what plan you're on. It's not a technicality, it's data protection law, and you're the one who answers for it. What does work: swap real names for Client A and Client B, remove ID numbers and phone numbers, and paste only what the problem actually needs. Almost always the AI helps just as well with the disguised data, because what you're asking for is the shape of the answer, not the people.
preguntas.corta: Not without removing names. Replace them with Client A and Client B.

preguntas.q: I'm not allowed to install anything on my work computer. Can I still do the course?
preguntas.a: You can, and you'll actually get quite far. Everything in the first few weeks happens inside the browser, without installing a single program and without anyone asking for the admin password. The day you want to see your project running on your own machine, you will need to install something, and at that point you'll need to ask for permission or use your computer at home. Two common-sense warnings if you work at a company: check its policy before pasting internal documents into an AI chat, and don't publish anything belonging to the company online without permission.
preguntas.corta: Yes. The first few weeks are all browser, no installs needed.

preguntas.q: Where exactly do I start? Tell me the first click.
preguntas.a: Open Lesson 1, What ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Really Are, and do the whole thing today. It's about twenty-five minutes and it saves you half the headaches that come later, because you finally understand why it sometimes makes things up. Before starting it, create a free account with just one of the three. And when you finish it, go to My Project and write two lines about what you want to build, even if you're not sure yet: the rest of the course makes a lot more sense once you have something of your own in mind.
preguntas.corta: Lesson 1, today. And a free account with just one AI.

preguntas.q: Do I have to do the lessons in order, or can I jump to the one I care about?
preguntas.a: In order, at least the first ten. They're numbered and each one assumes you know the previous one, so skipping the fundamentals to jump straight to the one that caught your eye is the fastest way to get stuck without knowing why. From there on, there are blocks you can take separately, depending on whether you want to build a website, automate things, or set up an agent. If you came here looking for something specific, use the search bar at the top and then go back to the order.
preguntas.corta: In order for the first ten. After that, pick your block.

preguntas.q: What's the Program, and how is it different from the Guides?
preguntas.a: The Program is the course in order: numbered lessons, each with its explanation and its tasks that you check off as you go. It's the path, and it's how you make progress. The Guides are something else: longer texts that take a whole topic and cover it from start to finish, meant to be read straight through when you want to fully understand something. There are guides about how this works under the hood, about which AI to use for what, about your first project, and about publishing online. When in doubt, always go with the Program; the Guides are the reinforcement.
preguntas.corta: The Program is the ordered path. The Guides are single-topic reads.

preguntas.q: What is the My Project section for?
preguntas.a: So the course stops being theory and starts being yours. There you answer four questions (what you want to build, for whom, what problem it solves, and what result would satisfy you), and the portal gives you back a brief you can copy and paste to the AI. It's also where the prompts you mark as useful get saved as you go. Fill it in early, even if it's half-finished and full of doubts: you can change it whenever you want, and working with a project of your own in mind completely changes what you get out of every lesson.
preguntas.corta: It's where you define what you'll build, and you can change it anytime.

preguntas.q: What are Prompts and the Institutional Kits?
preguntas.a: Prompts is a library of ready-made requests, ready to copy and paste into the text box of ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. Each one tells you when to use it, what you need to swap in for your own details, what it'll give you back, and what to do with that answer. You can save them to My Project with one button. The Institutional Kits are complete example projects, with their phases, their prompts, their legal side, and their cost: they're there to show you what a truly finished thing looks like. You'll use the prompts from week one; the kits, later on.
preguntas.corta: Prompts: ready-to-copy requests. Kits: complete example projects.

preguntas.q: And Tools and the Dictionary?
preguntas.a: Tools is the profile of each program that comes up in the course: what it does, what it's really good for, when it makes sense and when it doesn't. It's there so you can decide without wading through anyone's sales page. The Dictionary is exactly what it sounds like: an alphabetical list of the odd words you'll run into, with a one-line meaning, a comparison, and what not to confuse it with. When you read something and don't know what a port, a token, or a deployment is, you go there, check it in twenty seconds, and move on. You don't need to read it cover to cover.
preguntas.corta: Tools: program profiles. Dictionary: the odd words.

preguntas.q: What if I get stuck and have no one to ask?
preguntas.a: You have the AI itself, and it works better than it sounds. When something breaks, copy the whole message exactly as it is, without summarizing it, and paste it in with the same attitude you'd have showing an X-ray to a doctor: you don't need to understand it yourself. Ask it first to tell you what it thinks is wrong, before it touches anything. If you're still stuck, go back to the previous lesson, because the snag is almost always something from an earlier step that got left half-done. And if you've been going in circles for twenty minutes, stop and leave it for tomorrow: it's a small piece of advice that saves a lot of projects.
preguntas.corta: Paste the whole error to the AI and ask for the diagnosis first.
